The Boat-billed heron (Cochlearius cochlearius) is a distinctive nocturnal wader inhabiting mangrove swamps and freshwater wetlands from Mexico to Argentina. A comprehensive field study examining incubating eggs maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] documented that the incubation period, or age at hatching, lasts approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days], though some broods in naturally fluctuating nest cavities hatched slightly earlier, between 21 and 25 days [ab = between 21 and 25 days]. This relatively short incubation period is typical of tropical ardeids and is likely an adaptation to high nest predation pressure. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings are brooded continuously by both parents, and their initial wet body mass averages 32.5 grams [Ww0 = 32.5 grams], representing a modest investment in yolk reserves that transitions rapidly to exogenous feeding. The chicks are fed regurgitated fish and crustaceans, initiating the exotrophic transition within the first few days of life.

As the nestlings develop under the warm thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, approximately 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones unfolds. The wet weight at birth is 24.3 grams [Wwb = 24.3 grams], recorded immediately after hatching before any feeding, a value that reflects the depletion of yolk reserves during the final stages of embryonic development. This neonatal mass is notably lower than the initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg of 32.5 grams [Ww0 = 32.5 grams], indicating substantial metabolic consumption during organogenesis and albumen absorption. The chicks grow rapidly on a protein-rich diet, achieving their flight feathers and reaching the fledgling stage at 40 days after hatching [tx = 40 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This fledging period is consistent with other medium-sized herons and is followed by a short period of post-fledging dependence during which the young continue to be provisioned by the parents while refining their foraging skills.

Reproductive maturity in the Boat-billed heron follows a markedly different timeline when examined under the same thermal regime of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. Young individuals attain puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activity and the development of secondary sexual characteristics, at 120 days after hatching [tp = 120 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This relatively early sexual maturation is somewhat unusual among ardeids, many of which delay puberty into their second year, and may reflect the species' tropical distribution where extended breeding seasons relax selection for deferred reproduction. However, first reproduction is typically deferred considerably beyond the point of physiological maturity. Field observations indicate that females do not produce their first brood until approximately 730 days after hatching [tR = approximately 730 days after hatching], a delay that likely reflects the time required to establish a breeding territory and accumulate sufficient body condition to sustain the energetic demands of incubation and chick provisioning at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C].

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species, a pattern common among herons that may be linked to differential parental roles. The wet weight at ultimate size for females reaches a maximum of 602 grams [Wwi = 602 grams], whereas males attain a substantially larger adult mass of 712 grams [Wwi = 712 grams]. This approximately 18% size difference is likely related to male-male competition for nesting sites and the physical demands of territory defense, as males engage in aerial displays and aggressive encounters along mangrove channels. Female body mass, by contrast, is constrained by the energetic costs of egg production; a clutch typically contains 2.8 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2.8 eggs per clutch], representing a significant reproductive investment relative to maternal body size. The species produces just a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a conservative reproductive strategy that may be linked to the extended period of biparental care required by the altricial young.

Longevity records for the Boat-billed heron indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 4,234 days [am = approximately 4,234 days], based on long-term banding studies conducted in Costa Rican mangrove systems at typical ambient temperatures of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This lifespan is modest compared to larger ardeids such as the Great Blue Heron, which can exceed 20 years, but is consistent with the faster pace of life history expected in a relatively small-bodied tropical species with high juvenile mortality. Senescent adult mortality typically occurs after reproductive output has declined, with few individuals surviving beyond their tenth year. Taken together, the life history traits of Cochlearius cochlearius — relatively rapid development to fledging, early puberty, delayed first reproduction in favor of territory acquisition, a single annual clutch of moderate size, and a maximum lifespan of about 4,234 days — describe a species adapted to stable tropical wetlands where competition for high-quality nesting sites is intense but adult survival is moderate.
